headline: Apple updates App Store rules to explicitly ban 'nudify' AI apps and 'bait-and-switch' tactics
summary: The new guidelines target apps generating nonconsensual intimate imagery and those changing features post-approval, following recent criticism.
details: Apple has officially updated its App Store rules to explicitly prohibit "nudify" apps that use AI to create nonconsensual intimate images. This move clarifies content moderation requirements, mandating developers to proactively prevent and remove such content.

The rule changes come after significant criticism earlier this year, including incidents where X users utilized Grok to generate nonconsensual deepfakes. Protests at WWDC and a San Francisco city attorney's order also called for the removal of such apps.

Developers who fail to implement adequate safeguards or do not remedy violations after notice risk removal from the App Store. Apple also clarified rules against "bait-and-switch" apps, which add or change features, including "nudification," after initial approval.

Furthermore, the updated guidelines more clearly state that any apps facilitating human trafficking or the exploitation of children will be pulled from the App Store and blocked from alternative distribution channels.

headline_marked: [[AI agents' X impressions plummeted 98.7%]] after replies were cut, from 447K to 5K daily
headline: AI agents' X impressions plummeted 98.7% after replies were cut, from 447K to 5K daily
summary: An experiment found that AI agents drove over 1.1M X impressions in 5 days, but cutting their replies caused a 98.7% drop. It also revealed how bots can inflate e-commerce checkout data.
details: An experiment tracking AI agents on a personal X account saw daily impressions drop from a peak of 447,575 to just 5,686 after AI-generated replies were stopped. This represents a 98.7% decrease, demonstrating the critical role replies played in reach.

The "Can my AI agents make me famous?" experiment began on October 10, with AI agents taking over the @mattbusel X account. Within four days, the account crossed one million impressions, primarily driven by replies to large threads.

Impressions peaked on October 13 with 447,575 views, coinciding with 125 replies sent by agents. After replies ceased on October 15, impressions sharply declined, illustrating a direct correlation between agent activity and visibility.

The experiment also uncovered a "plot twist" in e-commerce: Stripe logged 1,865 checkout sessions in one day, but almost all were generated by the agents themselves. Only 23 sessions were potentially human, with zero paid transactions.

This inflated data was due to buy links being plain GET links that created a Stripe checkout session whenever anything opened them, including agents verifying their own links, monitors, crawlers, or link preview bots. The funnel appeared busy but meant nothing.

Lessons learned include tagging agent requests to filter them from counts, making buy URLs a page with a button instead of a direct session link, and only counting payment_status = paid. It also highlighted the need to treat bursts of sessions as robotic until proven otherwise.
